This convention is so ingrained that violating it feels disorienting. 219 220 Use the `transitionTypes` prop on `` to tag forward navigations: 221 222 ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 223 224 {/* photo thumbnail */} 225 226 ``` 227 228 The same pattern works for any navigation within the app. For example, previous/next arrows on a photo detail page can use `nav-back` and `nav-forward` to animate in the corresponding direction. 229 230 For links that return the user to a previous page, use `nav-back`: 231 232 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 233 234 ← Gallery 235 236 ``` 237 238 The transition type is not automatic. You decide which links are "forward" and which are "back" based on your app's navigation hierarchy. 239 240 Then wrap page content in a `ViewTransition` that maps transition types to directional animations: 241 242 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 243 256 {/* page content */} 257 258 ``` 259 260 The `enter` and `exit` props accept an object keyed by transition type. When a navigation carries the `nav-forward` type, the exit animation slides old content left and the enter animation slides new content in from the right. The `default: "none"` ensures that transitions without a type (browser back/forward, `router.refresh()`, Suspense reveals) produce no directional animation. 261 262 Wrap every participating page the same way. For the gallery to slide out on forward navigation and back in on `nav-back`, its page needs the same wrapper. Put the wrapper in each `page.tsx`, not the layout. Layouts persist across navigations, so enter and exit never fire there: 263 264 ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" 265 278 279 280 ``` 281 282 The CSS for directional slides: 283 284 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 285 ::view-transition-old(.nav-forward) { 286 --slide-offset: -60px; 287 animation: 288 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 289 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 290 } 291 ::view-transition-new(.nav-forward) { 292 --slide-offset: 60px; 293 animation: 294 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 295 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 296 } 297 298 ::view-transition-old(.nav-back) { 299 --slide-offset: 60px; 300 animation: 301 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 302 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 303 } 304 ::view-transition-new(.nav-back) { 305 --slide-offset: -60px; 306 animation: 307 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 308 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 309 } 310 311 @keyframes slide { 312 from { 313 translate: var(--slide-offset); 314 } 315 to { 316 translate: 0; 317 } 318 } 319 ``` 320 321 The 60px offset is enough to communicate direction without making the user track a fast-moving element across the screen. 322 323 #### Anchoring the header 324 325 During directional slides, the header should not move. A sliding header breaks the user's spatial anchor. They need one fixed reference point to understand that the _content_ moved, not the entire viewport. 326 327 Assign the header a `viewTransitionName` and suppress its animation in CSS: 328 329 ```tsx filename="components/header.tsx" 330
331 {/* navigation links */} 332
333 ``` 334 335 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 336 ::view-transition-group(site-header) { 337 animation: none; 338 z-index: 100; 339 } 340 ::view-transition-old(site-header) { 341 display: none; 342 } 343 ::view-transition-new(site-header) { 344 animation: none; 345 } 346 ``` 347 348 The `display: none` on the old snapshot prevents a flash where both old and new headers are briefly visible. The `z-index: 100` ensures the header renders above the sliding content. 349 350 If we navigate forward to a photo, content slides left. If we click the "← Gallery" link (tagged with `nav-back`), content slides right. The header stays fixed throughout both transitions. 351 352 Browser-initiated back navigations (the back button or swipe gestures) do not carry a transition type, so the directional slide does not play. The shared element morph from Step 1 still applies if both pages have matching `name` props. 353 354 #### Keeping the page interactive 355 356 While a transition runs, the `::view-transition` overlay captures pointer events, so clicks during the animation are lost. Let them pass through to the live page: 357 358 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 359 ::view-transition { 360 pointer-events: none; 361 } 362 ``` 363 364 This restores interactivity for unnamed content. Hit-testing still skips named participants (like the anchored header) for the transition's duration, so keep transitions short and avoid naming elements the user clicks rapidly. 365 366 #### Respecting reduced motion 367 368 Directional slides simulate physical movement across the viewport. This is the most common trigger for motion sensitivity. Morphs, reveals, and crossfades carry less risk since they affect smaller areas or rely on opacity rather than position. 369 370 The simplest approach is to disable all animation durations: 371 372 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 373 @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { 374 ::view-transition-old(*), 375 ::view-transition-new(*), 376 ::view-transition-group(*) { 377 animation-duration: 0s !important; 378 animation-delay: 0s !important; 379 } 380 } 381 ``` 382 383 Without animation, content swaps instantly, which is the browser's default behavior. Only the photo grid transitions between states. 418 419 ## Next steps 420 421 You now know how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation.
